title: Request-level trace correlation for metric-driven SLO reconstruction and anomaly gating
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Goal: Attach a lightweight request provenance token to incoming requests and propagate it through metrics and logs so that metric series can be reconstructed per-request for precise SLO attribution and to gate anomaly detectors before paging.

Why: Current burn-rate alerts and anomaly detection operate on aggregated series without robust request correlation. That leads to noisy pages during transient infrastructure events (noisy neighbors, GC storms) and makes root-cause attribution slow. By correlating traces to metrics and logs we can: (1) reconstruct SLO violations at request granularity, (2) compute burn-rate with exact request counts instead of sampled estimates, and (3) run anomaly models that consider request shapes and trace metadata to reduce false positives.

Design summary:
- Add an optional header X-RW-CTX (64-bit hex token) emitted by the API gateway for incoming requests; populate in SDKs for direct customers.
- Propagate X-RW-CTX through internal services via existing tracing context (W3C traceparent). If traceparent exists, derive X-RW-CTX deterministically from trace-id.
- Enrich metric points emitted by our runtime (latency histograms, request counters, error counters) with x_rw_ctx_tag dimension in the metrics ingestion pipeline (Vector -> Ingest Cluster). The tag will be added at the metrics shipper level to avoid touching every instrumented library.
- Augment logs with x_rw_ctx when present (Fluentd filter).
- Add a lightweight reconstruction pipeline in Observability that temporarily groups metrics/logs by x_rw_ctx for 2 minutes to compute per-request SLO outcome and feed the burn-rate calculator and anomaly detector. This pipeline keeps an eviction TTL and is storage-efficient (only metadata + counters).

Acceptance criteria:
- Ingest pipeline carries x_rw_ctx tag for >95% of requests through canary services.
- New burn-rate alert policy demonstrates 35% fewer pager opens in the canary window vs baseline for the same incidents.
- Anomaly detector uses per-request shape features and reduces false-positive rate by >=20% on historical replay.
- Runbook and dashboard for tracing-to-metrics correlation published (doc + dashboard links).

Trade-offs and risks:
- Privacy/PII: x_rw_ctx must never carry user-identifiable data. Design uses a derived opaque token; security review required for token derivation logic.
- Cost: retaining short-lived per-request state increases ingestion CPU and memory; we mitigate by TTL-limited aggregation and only enabling for services tagged as "slo-sensitive" initially.
- Backfill complexity: historical SLO reconstructions will be approximate; we will run model replay on one-week window to estimate improvements before a full rollout.

Rollout plan:
1) Implementation in runtime + shipper and internal canary for two low-traffic services (week 1).
2) Enable reconstruction pipeline for canary services and compare burn-rate alerts (week 2).
3) Expand to all SLO-critical services after observed improvement and operational runbook updates (week 3-4).

Monitoring & metrics we will add: percentage of requests with x_rw_ctx, per-service reconstruction hit rate, additional ingestion CPU/memory, false-positive rate of anomaly detector (replay), burn-rate alert pager count.

Notes on compatibility: If a service does not propagate x_rw_ctx, we will fall back to trace-id derivation where available. If neither exists, requests are treated as uncorrelated and will not be used in per-request reconstruction (will still be counted in coarse SLO metrics).
